sources.title: Sofonisba Anguissola (Q236038), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-20): English label 'Sofonisba Anguissola', description 'Italian painter (c.1532-1625)', instance of human, birth year recorded as 1530, 1531 and 1532 (1532 preferred), death recorded in 1625 (one value 16 November 1625), Korean label 소포니스바 안귀솔라. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Diane Moody, 'Anguissola, Sofonisba (1532-1625)', Women in World History: A Biographical Encyclopedia (Gale; reproduced on Encyclopedia.com; read in full). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: calls her a portrait painter who worked at the Spanish court of Philip II and the first professional woman artist of the Italian Renaissance, and follows her from training with Campi and Gatti, through the 1555 chess-game picture praised by Vasari and the Michelangelo exchange, the Spanish court from 1559 and two marriages to Genoa, Palermo and Van Dyck's 1624 visit. Draws mostly on Ilya Perlingieri's 1992 biography, which makes strong claims for her and for attributions; used with that in mind.

Angiola Maria Romanini, 'Anguissola, Sofonisba', Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, vol. 3 (Istituto della Enciclopedia Italiana Treccani, 1961; read in full, in Italian). INDEPENDENT AND RESTRAINED VOICE: documents her schooling with Campi (1545-49) and Gatti, her letter to Campi of 21 October 1561, Salviati's 1554 praise, Vasari's 1568 account of the chess picture and of the Michelangelo-circle drawing, the invitation to Madrid in 1559, the loss of nearly all her Spanish work, and Van Dyck's sketch of her in Palermo; judges her work to show a monotonous vein and modest limits, yet fresh and often witty observation in her portraits, and notes that her birth year is disputed.

Helene Meyer, 'Anguissola Sofonisba', French Ministry of Culture web feature on women artists (1 June 2018; read in full, in French). Independent institutional account: one of the first recognised women portraitists in Europe, the eldest of six daughters trained by Campi and Gatti, invited to Madrid in 1559 as lady-in-waiting and drawing teacher to the queen; adds a critical note that her career depended on her father and family, who took her commissions, and that she had neither the freedom to sell her canvases nor a studio; describes her portraits as sober with attention to the sitter's gaze and meticulous costumes, with about fifteen self-portraits; notes her Spanish work was long attributed to Sanchez Coello.

Alessandra Pagano, 'This Italian artist became the first female superstar of the Renaissance', National Geographic History magazine, 24 March 2022 (read in full). Magazine feature: her name and family, training under Campi and Gatti, the 1555 chess picture, the Michelangelo drawing request as reported in a 1562 letter to Cosimo de' Medici, the Spanish court and Queen Isabel, her marriages and Genoa, plus a section on works wrongly attributed to Sanchez Coello and a 2019 study that took 'Lady in a Fur Wrap' away from both El Greco and Anguissola.

The Art Story, 'Sofonisba Anguissola' (art-history encyclopedia entry with biography, read in full). Secondary compilation: her humanist education, apprenticeship in Campi's household from 1545, the portrait of the miniaturist Giulio Clovio in 1556, her service to Queen Elisabeth of Valois, the later marriage over her family's disapproval, the salon in Genoa, and Van Dyck's 1624 visit. Some dates differ from other sources (the marriage and her husband's death), so only points on which sources agree are used.

Cassandra Lee Tellier, 'Sofonisba Anguissola', EBSCO Research Starters (2024; read in full). Short scholarly biography with a bibliography led by the 1995 National Museum of Women in the Arts catalogue: innovative naturalistic portraits and family genre scenes, the Spanish court period and the change in her style, the difficulty of identifying her Spanish work (she rarely signed and did not take payment as a noblewoman), the Genoa salon, and Van Dyck's sketchbook drawing of her in her nineties.

Kunsthistorisches Museum Vienna, object record 'Self Portrait' by Sofonisba Anguissola, around 1554, miniature-format oil on poplar (read in full). Museum text: she was internationally renowned as a portrait painter to the end of her long life, spent 1560-72 at the Spanish court as lady-in-waiting and drawing teacher of the queen, and in this small self-portrait points at her name in the book she holds; the museum reads it as reflecting the seriousness and ethos of her art, the faithful, unvarnished rendering of nature. Used for scope and as a museum characterisation of her method.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_sofonisba_womenworld, src_sofonisba_treccani, src_sofonisba_ebsco, src_sofonisba_natgeo | 1551-1559 | reference biography, national biographical dictionary, scholarly biography, magazine feature] Vasari, writing in 1568, said her picture of her sisters playing chess made them seem alive; later writers call it an early conversation piece, and a drawing of a laughing girl and her answer to Michelangelo's request for a weeping boy (a 1562 letter to Cosimo de' Medici reports the request) were circulated by Michelangelo's friends. The Italian dictionary credits fresh, witty observation in her portraits but also a monotonous vein and modest limits, which tempers the pioneering claims in the encyclopedia and the magazine. CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 66 / 0.54 to 62 / 0.48 because the 'pioneer' wording comes from one lineage of recent admirers and the restrained Italian dictionary disagrees.

mastery_orientation.rationale: [src_sofonisba_womenworld, src_sofonisba_treccani, src_sofonisba_artstory, src_sofonisba_khm | 1545-1624 | reference biography, national biographical dictionary, art-history encyclopedia, museum record] She trained with Campi from about 1545 and with Gatti after he left, received advice from Michelangelo through letters her father supervised, painted a portrait of the miniaturist Giulio Clovio in 1556 in thanks for his advice, preferred to paint from life, and in 1624 gave Van Dyck hints on painting and talked about the true principles of the art (Van Dyck's sketchbook note, reported by three of the sources). The museum describes her method as the unvarnished rendering of nature. The Van Dyck conversation is one primary note retold, and the contacts with masters were arranged by her father. CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 64 / 0.50 to 60 / 0.44 because the late-life evidence is one primary note retold, and the exchanges with masters were managed by her father.

adaptability.rationale: [src_sofonisba_ebsco, src_sofonisba_treccani, src_sofonisba_artstory, src_sofonisba_ministry | 1559-1620 | scholarly biography, national biographical dictionary, art-history encyclopedia, institutional feature] She left Cremona for the Spanish court around 1559-60 and stayed over a decade as lady-in-waiting, drawing teacher and portraitist, then lived in Sicily, Genoa and Palermo; the scholarly biography notes a marked change from family scenes to court portraits that kept more personality than official models, and her later portraits are described as more fluid. Moves and roles were set largely by the king, her husbands and her family, so this shows how she worked within changing situations rather than that she sought them. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 62 / 0.48 to 58 / 0.44 because the major changes of place were arranged by others.

detail_orientation.rationale: [src_sofonisba_womenworld, src_sofonisba_treccani, src_sofonisba_ministry, src_sofonisba_ebsco | 1555-1560s | reference biography, national biographical dictionary, institutional feature, scholarly biography] Vasari called the chess picture most carefully finished; the Italian dictionary notes minute descriptive detail in the Nivaagaard family group; the French ministry notes her attachment to the careful rendering of costumes, and the scholarly biography speaks of miniaturist detail in her fluid style. The evidence is mainly about the finish of the work, not documented working habits.

persistence.rationale: [src_sofonisba_womenworld, src_sofonisba_ebsco, src_sofonisba_ministry | 1555-1624 | reference biography, scholarly biography, institutional feature] Sources describe a career of about seventy years, with self-portraits across her life (the last around 1620), and Van Dyck's 1624 note that her greatest sorrow was no longer being able to paint because of failing sight. Longevity and patrons' support also explain the span, and none of the sources describes how she handled setbacks, so this is an inference.

portrait.source: Self-portrait at the easel, oil on canvas, by Sofonisba Anguissola, Muzeum-Zamek w Lancucie (Lancut Castle Museum), inventory S.916ML; image is the museum's own front-of-painting photograph (2152 x 2500 pixels, file s916mc581-06574.jpg) offered for download on the museum's record on the Polish museums portal In Museums (wmuzeach.pl / inmuseums.pl), where each image carries a Public Domain Mark. Downscaled to 861 x 1000, not cropped, not upscaled; the portal's separate 26795 x 29689 'gigapixel' file was not used.

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: Stage B PLAUSIBLE (downgraded from strong; holder terms unread) / LEAD SURVIVED, with the holder record and terms now read. Lead: self-portrait at the easel, Lancut Castle Museum (Commons file from a Nivaagaard press page). At preflight the holder record (wmuzeach.pl) could not be opened (certificate error through the page reader); it opens with a plain request, so I read it: the museum record gives author Anguissola, inventory S.916ML, owner Castle Museum in Lancut, 67 x 56 cm, oil on wood and canvas, a popularisation note calling it a self-portrait of Sophonisba Anguissola and dating it 1554, a dating field 'sixteenth/seventeenth century', and a Public Domain Mark on each of three images (front, reverse, gigapixel). Reverse photograph shows a loan label naming 'Anguissola Sofonisba, Autoritratto al cavalletto' for a 2007-08 Milan exhibition. Portal Terms of Use (the portal is run by the Museum of King Jan III's Palace at Wilanow; read in full) contain no reuse restriction on images. The Lancut museum's own site (regulamin pages read) restricts visitor photography on its premises to personal non-commercial use, which does not govern a Public Domain Mark image the holder itself published; the holder's reproduction terms beyond the record were not found. TERMS CHECKED: yes, record plus portal terms; no permission, fee or restriction found; the one caveat is the museum's absent separate reuse policy. DATE DISCREPANCY: holder note 1554, holder date field 16th/17th century, Commons, French ministry and Rijksmuseum 1556 or 1556-57; recorded as c. 1556. SITTER: the holder calls it a self-portrait; the French Ministry of Culture captions the same picture 'Autoportrait, 1556, Lancut, chateau'; no inscription on the front (checked on the photograph). I used the holder's own image, not the Commons upload (6100 x 7087, Nivaagaard press source), and the Commons file page gave 'Copyright expired' only through a third party. Fallbacks checked and not used: Kunsthistorisches Museum self-portrait c.1554 (inscribed; page says private use only, reproduction request for commercial or academic use); Museum of Fine Arts Boston miniature (terms say commercial use prohibited; item record 403); Fondation Custodia (bot challenge); Van Dyck's Knole portrait (attributed, terms unread). REGION southern_europe; ERA early_modern; nationality IT (Cremona, then the Spanish Habsburg world). BIRTH YEAR 1532 is the Wikidata preferred value; sources vary (1527-28, 1530, 1531-32, 1531/35). ZERO POLITICS: painter and court portraitist; the Spanish court appears only as employer. KO NAME: 소포니스바 안귀솔라 is the Korean Wikipedia title and the Wikidata ko label. ATTRIBUTION: attributable (Vasari, letters, court documents), but many Spanish-period works are lost or misattributed, so scoring uses her documented career and not disputed pictures. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Women in World History entry (src_sofonisba_womenworld), with the Treccani dictionary as a restrained second voice. READ (7 sources besides Wikidata): Women in World History (full), Treccani DBI (full), French Ministry of Culture (full), National Geographic (full), The Art Story (full), EBSCO Research Starters (full), KHM record (full). Wikipedia opened for orientation only, not cited. NOT OPENED: Perlingieri 1992, Ferino-Pagden and Kusche 1995, Vasari's text itself, Van Dyck's sketchbook, Prado (bot wall), Britannica (bot wall). CONTRADICTIONS: marriage dates (1570/1571/1573; remarriage 1579/1580), who approved the second marriage (Art Story: king approved and family objected; EBSCO: over her brother's objection and without the king's permission), whether she went to Rome in 1554 (WWH and the ministry say so; the Italian dictionary does not), birth year, and whether the 'court painter' label fits (the portal note says she could not be court painter as a noblewoman). No dates of these are carded. Family concentration: five source families (Perlingieri lineage via encyclopedia, magazine and Art Story; the Italian dictionary; the French ministry; the 2024 scholarly summary; the KHM record). MAJOR ACHIEVEMENT GATE: PASS (cards: international fame as a portraitist from a noble family, with the chess-game picture and the Michelangelo exchange; her years as portraitist to the Spanish court; the self-portraits, the largest set by any woman of her time and a career of about seventy years). SELF-CALIBRATION: 5 initial rows; 3 lowered (creative originality, mastery orientation, adaptability), none raised, 2 reviewed and kept (detail orientation, persistence); of the three, 2 were concentration lowerings (creative originality, mastery orientation) and 1 self-calibration (adaptability).
